item.title: Interpret how an archive treats a missing letter
item.summary: An archivist explains why a blank in a record can have several meanings.
item.transcript_text:
Listener: The tenant's letter isn't in the file. Does that mean it never reached the office?
Archivist: It might never have been sent. It might have been answered without being filed. Or it might be elsewhere, with records of the person who received it. The archive preserves an administrative route through the story.
Listener: Then why show the absence at all?
Archivist: Otherwise, it's easy to take the landlord's account for the only one anyone gave. We have a copy of a reply that refers to a complaint. It doesn't repeat the complaint's words. Showing that copy makes it possible to say exactly what is supported and what remains open, without claiming to recover a lost voice.

questions.prompt: What overly strong inference does the archivist reject?
options: The surviving accounts reflect unequal preservation
The letter never arrived because it is absent here
Records can be filed in different places
Some absences matter enough to label
questions.explanation: Several plausible filing and communication paths could explain the absence.

questions.prompt: What does an administrative route suggest?
options: Record-keeping captures particular processes and viewpoints
A floor plan of the office survives
Tenants had a separate physical entrance
The archives document only staff shifts
questions.explanation: The surviving arrangement cannot stand for everyone involved.

questions.prompt: What does the copy of the reply support?
options: The tenant certainly wrote the reply
The original letter has been located
The landlord never gave an account
A complaint is referred to, but its precise wording is unavailable
questions.explanation: The reply points to a complaint without preserving its words.

options: To accuse the office of deliberately removing a file
To explain the name of the archivist
Otherwise readers may assume no competing account existed
To persuade the landlord to send another note
questions.explanation: An unmarked gap can make surviving material seem more complete than it is.

questions.prompt: Which method does the archivist advocate?
options: Write a likely complaint in the tenant’s voice
Display the trace along with its limits
Treat every possibility as equally evidenced
Remove the reply for fairness
questions.explanation: The reply supplies evidence whose reach can be stated carefully.
